title: Substack Surfacer: countering Substack overwhelm
subtitle: A Python script to rank Substack posts by likes per subscriber
description: A Python script to rank Substack posts by likes per subscriber
truncated_body_text: There was a golden age of Substack where I subscribed to <50 newsletters, and I could more or less read everything I wanted to. Now, however, I subscribe to >200, and I just don’t have time to keep up.
body_html:
There was a golden age of Substack where I subscribed to <50 newsletters, and I could more or less read everything I wanted to. Now, however, I subscribe to >200, and I just don’t have time to keep up.

Enter: Substack Surfacer, a Python script I created that produces CSVs like this with the posts from all of the Substacks you follow, in a form that makes it easy to sort by the number of likes or (even more useful) the number of likes per subscriber (since of course, newsletters with more subscribers tend to get more likes).

Right now it requires basic knowledge of Python (pip install), and it can take a while to complete due to Substack’s rate limiting (about an hour per 100 newsletters).

Some of the posts from the last couple of months that it helped me surface:

  • Death of a knowledge system (331 likes from 759 free subscribers) and Birth of the Wisdom Economy (122 likes from 759 free subscribers) by

  • Deep AF Green by (16 likes from 182 free subscribers)

  • Finding balance with technology by (6 likes from 94 free subscribers)

  • Becoming Soul (24 likes from 269 free subscribers) by

  • Live threads through my favorite city — London (14 likes from 107 free subscribers) by

  • How to Start a School With Your Friends (96 likes from ~1,000 free subscribers) by

Let me know if you find it useful!

Best,
Stephen

What I’ve been up to

  • and I published Chapter 1: The Techno-Skeptics and Chapter 2, part 1: The Techno-Optimists: e/acc of Technological Metamodernism

  • I spent a very full month at Emerge Lakefront, including celebrating midsummer and participating in a week-long residency on Network Nations

  • Laura and I holidayed for a week in Skåne, where highlights included the coastal Stenshuvud National Park, Ales Stenar (the ‘Swedish Stonehenge’), cute Österlen villages lined with wild hollyhocks and Malmö’s lively Folkets Park

Plans for the future

  • A Swedish B2 course at Folkuniversitet, 18-29 Aug

  • Spark Changemakers on Ekskäret, 9-13 Sep

  • Deep Joy: A Samadhi Retreat with Yahel Avigur and Sari Markkanen in Finland, 15-22 Sep

Some tips for the LLM connoisseur

  • EQ-Bench Longform Creative Writing is one of the most meaningful AI benchmarks to me. Sonnet 3.7 ranks above Sonnet 4, with a slop score second only to Opus 4, which fits with the fact that Sonnet 3.7 (thinking) is still my favourite AI writing partner (adjusting for cost – I can’t justify the huge extra cost of Opus 4 for the marginal benefit).

  • The Chinese open-source labs have been absolutely cooking though, with Kimi K2, Qwen3 235B A22B Thinking 2507 and Qwen3 Coder looking incredibly strong.

  • To see what models have product-market fit, check OpenRouter’s weekly chart. To see what’s hot, check the trending chart.

  • Don’t compare the cost of reasoning and non-reasoning models using per-token pricing, as (by design) reasoning models output way more tokens. A better indicator of cost is the Cost to Run Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (note the log scale on the x-axis).

  • Dandelion’s current workhorse is Gemini 2.5 Flash, in standard and thinking variants.

Note: Qwen3 235B (Reasoning) shown here is the original version, not the just-released 2507 version. I expect the 2507 version to be on the intelligence-cost frontier.

Offerings from friends

Dandelion is closing on £5m tickets sold. Why not list your next event there?

  • Breadchain friends will be at the Crypto Commons Gathering in Austria at the Commons Hub, 24-29 Aug 🍞

  • Join jae spencer-keyse, Jan Baeriswyl and Dominique Antonina for the fourth Futurecraft Residency, this time taking place at The Garden near Porto, Portugal, 2-8 Sep 🌿

title: In Correspondence #54
subtitle: 40 years, Anki and Cursor
body_html:
What I’ve been up to

  • I celebrated my 40th birthday with friends on Viggsö (a wedding present, thank you Harry!)

  • I was very impressed with the Nobel Week Lights in Stockholm

  • Laura and I enjoyed an evening at Yasuragi (another wedding present, thank you friends!)

  • I spent a few days in London, primarily to visit my new baby niece. I also dropped into E5 Bakehouse · 21Sid · Finch · London Fields Lido · Coal Drops Yard · Mare St. Market · Limehouse Library Hotel spa

  • and I published several more chapters of the Technological Metamodernism book:

    • What is Technology?

    • What is Metamodernism?

    • Proto-metamodern thinkers on technology

    • d/acc

How I use Anki

I’ve now learnt 5000 Swedish words with Anki. This is my current setup, evolved over the past few years:

  • For the actual cards, I downloaded the Swedish Kelly word list, a freely available frequency-based vocabulary list, and then used AI (Google Gemini Flash) to create examples sentences for each word

  • I use two addons:

    • Pass/Fail to reduce the overwhelming default of four options (Again, Easy, Good, Hard) down to just two

    • HyperTTS with realtime Google Chirp 3 to speak the sentences out loud

  • I check dubious translations using DeepL for macOS with the ⌘CC ‘copy to translate’ shortcut

  • If I have questions, I use the ChatGPT macOS app via the ⌥ + space shortcut

I find I can reliably review 150 cards and learn 30 new words in a 30 minute session.

How I use Cursor

I used over half a billion tokens in Cursor in 2025, mainly on improving Dandelion (which has now been used to sell 150,000 tickets worth almost £5.5m)

  • With Tool AI/Keep the Future Human in mind, I use the editor/code-centric view (rather than the agent view)

  • Key shortcuts:

    • ⌘L: add selection to context (followed by ⌘N if I want to clear previous context)

    • ⌘/: change model (Composer 1 is my default, I switch to Opus 4.5 for tough questions)

  • When working on Dandelion, before I commit, I often use my /diff slash command to Run `git diff`, inspect any altered files and verify the changes look good to commit. A commit and push then triggers the test suite to be run as a matrix on Github Actions (setup here).

  • I commit using OpenCommit with commit messages provided by moonshotai/kimi-k2-0905:nitro on OpenRouter (as a small way of supporting open source AI)

What I’ve been reading/watching

  • The Thinking Game documentary on Demis Hassabis/Google DeepMind (see also his recent interview on the DeepMind channel)

  • Vitalik Buterin’s latest piece Let a thousand societies bloom

  • The Resonant Computing Manifesto

  • The Strange Physics That Gave Birth to AI, on spin glasses (which I did my dissertation on back in 2008!)

Offerings from friends

title: Fifteen things I'm really glad I did, and you could do too
subtitle: Ending with some wonderful news
truncated_body_text: Get seriously into meditation: Attend multi-day retreats in each of the areas listed on the Hermes Amara website (which could be condensed into four: Samādhi/Jhāna, Emptiness/Ways of Looking, Mettā, and Soulmaking). I can recommend retreats with Gaia House
body_html:
1. Get seriously into meditation: Attend multi-day retreats in each of the areas listed on the Hermes Amara website (which could be condensed into four: Samādhi/Jhāna, Emptiness/Ways of Looking, Mettā, and Soulmaking). I can recommend retreats with Gaia House and Nirodha

  2. Take up endurance sports: Enter a swimrun, triathlon or long-distance running, cycling or swimming race

  3. Keep a journal: Buy a quality journal and pen and aim to write a few pages every week

  4. Read widely: Including a healthy dose of protopian fiction like Retrotopia, A Psalm for the Wild-Built, Another Life and classics like Island and The Dispossessed

  5. Sing regularly: Join a choir, take singing lessons or attend an event like Voice Camp

  6. Learn a language: Start by finding the most common 5000 words in your target language and use AI to turn them into Anki flashcards

  7. Start a newsletter: Email is the original open, decentralised protocol. Having the email addresses of followers means you can move to another platform at will, without needing to rebuild your following. Options include Substack and Ghost

  8. Use the best versions of the latest AIs: Current top models are orders of magnitude more capable than those from a couple of years ago, and are also much more capable than current free versions. Use AI to help you write a book, create a film or make an album.

  9. Host an event: Run an event, online or offline, on a topic you’re passionate about. List it on Dandelion (no platform fees, run by a not-for-profit worker co-operative, fair source and open data)

  10. Start a co-op with your friends: Become your own bosses and work on something truly meaningful to you

  11. Join the Green Party (if you’re in the UK): The next UK election is just 3 years away, and for the first time ever, a Green-led government is a realistic possibility–but a Green win will require your participation

  12. Visit prefigurative spaces: Spend some time at places prototyping new ways of living and being like Brave Earth, Emerge Lakefront, Casa Tilo, Feÿtopia and Life Itself

  13. (Yet) Call somewhere home: Being a digital nomad was fun but it doesn’t compare to really planting roots somewhere (for me that somewhere was Totnes, now Stockholm). Prepare for the possibility that international travel becomes more difficult and expensive over the coming years.

  14. Get married: Something deep in my being has relaxed since getting married. describes it as a ‘magic spell’. Plus the wedding was incredibly fun.

  15. Have kids: Yes, I’m now a dad ☺️ Our daughter Runa was born on 2 March. So far I’m resonating with Having Kids Has Been Far Easier and Better than I Expected

Mettā,
Stephen

I’ll be taking on new coaching clients from April.

At the invitation of the organisers, I recorded a one-minute acceptance video which was shown at the awards ceremony.

What I’ve been reading/watching

  • Walking the New Camino by :

“For the past couple years Nati and I have been talking about the ‘New Camino’: a new generation of retreat centres, community hubs, and co-living spaces we see emerging across Europe. New spaces supporting a new kind of pilgrimage...”

  • Towards a more self-reflective Green politics by and Paul Powlesland:

“Some therefore suggest that building on the Green Party of England and Wales’s success will require a more self-aware political sensibility: a movement conscious of its own style, instincts and assumptions, and able to see its foundational values as partial and contextual even as it seeks to realise them. A Green politics shaped by greater awareness of its own worldview as construct, rather than reality itself - that can discern what’s valid in opponents’ perspectives without simply reproducing their frame.”

More articles on my knowledgegraph.

Plans for the future

body_html:
Dear friends,

You’re invited to join me and a fantastic lineup of special guests for a seven-week journey through Technological Metamodernism in association with the Emerge Institute, featuring:

  • , Co-author of Civic.AI and Plurality.net

  • , Founder of the P2P Foundation

  • Beatrice Erkers, Director of the Existential Hope program at the

  • , Co-founder of Casa Tilo, Loomio, Enspiral and Microsolidarity

  • (Hanzi Freinacht), Metamoderna

  • Indra Adnan, Founder of The Alternative

Ask what technology is doing to us and you tend to get one of two answers. Either it’s ruining us — our attention, our privacy, our politics — or it’s about to save us, if we can just build fast enough. Both sides are right about a great deal. Neither is adequate. And the argument between them has crowded out the questions that actually matter: what kinds of technology, built how, by whom, governed through what mechanisms, in service of what?

Technological Metamodernism is an attempt to answer those questions by adopting the metamodern mindset of openness, play and synthesis. Over seven weeks we’ll work through the debates, before turning to the alternatives now taking shape: d/acc‘s defensive, decentralising technologies; Plurality‘s tools for democratic coordination across difference; cosmo-localism‘s vision of local production drawing on a global knowledge commons. We'll ask why these approaches remain marginal, whether the real barrier is how we see the world, and the role of community in sustaining different ways of looking.

I hope to see many of you there!
